subject: Accounting
title: Value-Added Tax Explained
description: Learn Value-Added Tax Explained in one minute.

hook.text: Outside the U.S., most countries use a different system: the value-added tax, or VAT.

buildup.text: VAT is charged at every stage of production—from raw material to finished product.

discovery.text: Each business pays VAT on its purchases and charges VAT on its sales. The difference goes to the government.

twist.text: Unlike sales tax, VAT is harder to evade because every business in the chain reports it.

climax.text: Over 170 countries use VAT. The U.S. is the only major economy that doesn't.

punchline.text: VAT taxes the value each step adds to a product.

quiz.question: How does VAT differ from sales tax?
options: VAT is collected at every production stage, not just the final sale
VAT is lower than sales tax

details.summary: Value Added Tax is a consumption tax used by over 160 countries, collected at every stage of production by taxing only the value added at each step. Unlike sales tax, it is self-enforcing because businesses claim credits for VAT already paid.
details.whyItMatters: VAT is the world's most common consumption tax, generating about 20% of global tax revenue. Understanding it is essential for international business and for comparing tax systems across countries.
takeaways: VAT is collected at each stage of production, not just at the final sale like sales tax
Businesses pay VAT on inputs but claim credits, so only the value added at each stage is effectively taxed
Over 160 countries use VAT, making it the most widely adopted tax system in the world

faq.question: How is VAT different from sales tax?
faq.answer: Sales tax is collected only at the final sale. VAT is collected at every production stage, but businesses deduct VAT paid on inputs. The consumer bears the full tax either way, but VAT is harder to evade because each business in the chain must report to claim credits.

faq.question: Why do most countries use VAT instead of sales tax?
faq.answer: VAT is self-enforcing: businesses must report their purchases to claim input credits, creating a paper trail at every production stage. This makes evasion much harder than with sales tax, where only the final retailer reports. VAT also generates consistent revenue even with complex supply chains.
